methods.name: AR1-ZO
methods.full_name: AR1-ZO: Alternating Rank-1 Zeroth-Order optimisation of LoRA with topology-aware scaling
methods.paper_title: AR1-ZO: Topology-Aware Rank-1 Zeroth-Order Queries for High-Rank LoRA Fine-Tuning
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+\tfrac{\gamma}{r}BAx=W_0x+\alpha\sum_{k=1}^{r}b_k a_k^{\top}x,\ \ \gamma=\alpha r,\ \ B=[b_1,\dots,b_r]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A=[a_1,\dots,a_r]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\ \ \text{step } t:\ k(t)=1+(t\bmod r)\ (\text{same atom index in every adapted matrix}),\ \ z_t=(z_b,z_a)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d_{out}+d_{in}}),\ \ \ell_{\pm}=\mathcal{L}(\theta_t\pm\mu P_tz_t),\ \ \hat g_t=\frac{\ell_+-\ell_-}{2\mu}\,z_t=(\hat g_{b,t},\hat g_{a,t}),\ \ b_{k(t)}\leftarrow b_{k(t)}-\eta_t\hat g_{b,t},\ \ a_{k(t)}\leftarrow a_{k(t)}-\eta_t\hat g_{a,t};\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0 \text{ and every atom } j\neq k(t) \text{ (shared by both endpoints)};\ \text{trained: all } r \text{ atoms, one per step, from two forward passes and no backpropagation}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{stored per adapted matrix } (r=64 \text{ in the main runs});\ \text{only } d_{in}+d_{out} \text{ coordinates are perturbed and updated per step}
methods.locus: LoRA-adapted linear layers of OPT-2.7B/13B and Qwen3-1.7B/32B. The mechanism diagnostics use the 28 v_proj matrices of Qwen3-1.7B; the target modules of the main runs are not listed.
methods.structure:
The stored object is an ordinary rank-\(r\) LoRA delta \(\Delta W=\alpha\sum_k b_ka_k^{	op}\). AR1-ZO changes only how a two-point zeroth-order oracle measures it. Each query perturbs one matched rank-1 atom \((b_k,a_k)\), a block of dimension \(q=d_{out}+d_{in}\). Lemma 4.1 shows this is the smallest complete LoRA-native block: one-sided blocks miss part of the first-order variation \(\delta b_k a_k^{	op}+b_k\delta a_k^{	op}\). The estimator's dimension term is therefore \(q\), not \(rq\). The second ingredient is scale. Under the canonical coefficient \(\gamma/r=\alpha/r\), the active finite-difference signal is \(\Theta(1/r)\). Against a rank-independent evaluation-noise floor its SNR is \(\Theta(1/r^2)\), and \(\mathbb{E}\cos(\hat
abla_k\mathcal{L},
abla_k\mathcal{L})	o0\) once \(r\gg r_c=\Theta(\alpha\mu\|g\|/\sigma_\xi)\). The paper calls this directional collapse. Setting \(\gamma=\alpha r\) gives every queried atom the rank-free coefficient \(\alpha\). In forward-map terms, the method is LoRA with scale \(\alpha\) (instead of \(\alpha/r\) or \(\alpha/\sqrt r\)) trained by cyclic block-coordinate ZO over rank-1 atoms. Rank then appears only as coverage: over a cycle the stationarity measure is \(	frac1r\sum_k\|
abla_k\mathcal{L}\|^2\). The convergence bound assumes a stable represented-adapter scale, because the joint output scale under \(\gamma=\alpha r\) is not normalised by \(r\). A rank-\(m\) block query uses \(\gamma=\alpha r/m\) and has dimension \(mq\).
methods.mergeable_reason: The trained adapter is a plain additive delta \(\Delta W=\alpha BA\) and folds into \(W_0\) exactly like LoRA. The atom schedule and \(\gamma=\alpha r\) affect training only.
methods.identity_at_init: Yes. \(B\) is initialised at zero and \(A\) at random (Appendix B.1), so \(\Delta W=\alpha\sum_k b_ka_k^{\top}=0\) at step 0.
methods.key_idea: In zeroth-order LoRA, rank should set storage and coverage, not the dimension of each query or the signal it measures. AR1-ZO perturbs one complete rank-1 atom \((b_k,a_k)\) per two-forward-pass query and gives it the coefficient \(\gamma/r=\alpha\) instead of \(\alpha/r\). This removes the \(1/r^2\) decay of the finite-difference SNR that makes naive atomwise ZO collapse at high rank.
methods.results_note: With \(r=64\) on OPT-2.7B, AR1-ZO beats MeZO-LoRA on all six tasks, e.g. SQuAD F1 77.8 vs 64.6 and DROP 27.8 vs 23.9. The same atom schedule with canonical \(\alpha/r\) scaling (ZO-Alt-naive) collapses to 19.2 and 6.3.

relations.note: Uses the same two-point SPSA/RGE oracle on paired mini-batches, restricted to one LoRA atom per query.
Keeps the rank-r LoRA parameterisation and the B=0 init. Only the coefficient (gamma = alpha*r) and the per-step update set change.

Competing rank-scaling rule. rsLoRA uses alpha/sqrt(r) for joint first-order updates; AR1-ZO gives each queried atom the coefficient alpha. In the paper's SQuAD ablation, both alpha/r and alpha/sqrt(r) stagnate under atomwise ZO.

Another way to cut ZO perturbation dimension. AGZO perturbs in an activation-derived rank-r subspace of the dense weight; AR1-ZO uses the native LoRA atoms, with no auxiliary basis and no activation hooks.
Another 2026 low-dimensional ZO fine-tuning scheme, using a random rank-r subspace plus orthogonalisation. AR1-ZO instead exposes the stored LoRA atoms one at a time.

methods.name: Pico
methods.full_name: Pico: Pre-merge interference calibration in output-space
methods.paper_title: Crowded in B-Space: Calibrating Shared Directions for LoRA Merging
methods.formula_latex: \text{per layer and target module, with LoRAs } \Delta W_t=B_tA_t\ (t=1,\dots,T;\ \text{scale absorbed into } B_t):\ \ B_{\text{all}}=[B_1,\dots,B_T]=U\Sigma V^{\top},\ \ s_j=\frac{\sigma_j^2}{\sum_k\sigma_k^2},\ \ \alpha_j=\frac{1}{1+(T-1)s_j},\ \ S=I_{d_{out}}+U\,\mathrm{diag}(\alpha-\mathbf{1})\,U^{\top},\ \ \tilde B_t=SB_t;\ \ \Delta W_{\text{calib}}=\mathcal{M}\big(\tilde B_1A_1,\dots,\tilde B_TA_T\big)\ \ (\mathcal{M}\in\{\text{TA},\text{TIES},\text{TSV-M},\dots\}),\ \ \Delta W_{\text{Pico}}=\gamma\,\Delta W_{\text{calib}},\ \ \gamma=\frac{\tfrac1T\sum_t\|B_tA_t\|_F}{\|\Delta W_{\text{calib}}\|_F};\ \ W=W_0+\Delta W_{\text{Pico}};\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0 \text{ and all } A_t,B_t;\ \text{nothing is trained and no data is used}
methods.trainable_params: 0\ \text{(data-free post-hoc merge); per adapted matrix: one SVD of the } d_{out}\times Tr \text{ stack plus } T \text{ left multiplications}
methods.locus: Every LoRA-adapted matrix (q_proj and v_proj in the experiments) of Llama-3.1-8B, and of Qwen3-4B-Base in an appendix. Four domain LoRAs (math, code, finance, medical) of rank 8 to 64.
methods.structure: Pico left-multiplies each output factor, before merging, by one layer-wise operator \(S=U\,\mathrm{diag}(\alpha)\,U^{\top}+(I-UU^{\top})\). \(S\) is symmetric positive definite: its eigenvalues are \(\alpha_j\in[1/T,1]\) on \(\mathrm{col}(B_{\text{all}})\) and 1 on the orthogonal complement. It therefore shrinks output directions that carry a large share of the stacked \(B\) energy. The maximum shrinkage is \(1/T\), the factor by which averaging over-counts a direction shared by all \(T\) tasks. A single scalar \(\gamma\) then restores the mean source Frobenius norm. \(A_t\) is untouched; in the ablation, calibrating \(A\) or the full \(BA\) instead lowers accuracy. Two consequences are derived here. (i) Task Arithmetic is linear, so \(\mathcal{M}(SB_tA_t)=S\,\mathcal{M}(B_tA_t)\) and Pico-TA equals the post-merge output-space reshaping \(\gamma S\Delta W_{\text{TA}}\); applying \(S\) before merging matters only for non-linear mergers such as TIES and TSV-M. (ii) \(s_j\) is a direction's share of the stacked spectrum, only a proxy for cross-task sharing, so a direction dominated by one task's energy is shrunk too. \(U\) is the left singular basis of the concatenated \(B\)'s. It is the same output basis Core Space builds, and it spans the column space that KnOTS aligns in.
methods.mergeable_reason: The output is one additive delta per layer, \(\Delta W_{\text{Pico}}=\gamma\,\mathcal{M}(\{SB_tA_t\})\), of rank at most \(Tr\) for TA. It folds into \(W_0\) like any merged LoRA.
methods.identity_at_init: Nothing is trained. With a single adapter (\(T=1\)), every \(\alpha_j=1\), so \(S=I\), \(\gamma=1\) and \(\Delta W_{\text{Pico}}=B_1A_1\): the calibration is the identity in the one-task case.
methods.key_idea: Across independently trained LoRAs, the output factors \(B_t\) reuse a few shared directions: pairwise overlap \(O_B\gg O_A\), and the effective rank of \(B\) is about 3 at LoRA rank 64. A linear merge counts these directions \(T\) times. Pico shrinks them before merging with the spectral weights \(\alpha_j=1/(1+(T-1)s_j)\) and then restores the update norm.
methods.results_note: On Llama-3.1-8B with four rank-16 domain LoRAs, Pico raises the eight-benchmark average from 0.4093 to 0.4430 under Task Arithmetic, from 0.3859 to 0.4328 under TIES and from 0.3473 to 0.4305 under TSV-M. Pico+TA (0.4430) also beats a jointly trained multi-task LoRA (0.3688).

relations.note: Plug-in calibration before TA (+3.4 points). For TA it equals left-multiplying the merged delta by S and rescaling.
Calibrated factors are then merged by TIES (+4.7 points average).
Calibrated factors are then merged by TSV-M (+8.3 points, the largest gain).

Both work in a shared output basis from an SVD over the stacked task updates. KnOTS aligns and then merges the task-specific input-side factors; Pico rescales the shared output directions by their energy share.
Uses the same left singular basis of the concatenated B's (Core Space's U_B), but calibrates in it instead of projecting to a small core. Core Space is a baseline that Pico beats in Table 1.
Sparsify-and-rescale interference reduction; a baseline in every merger block.
LoRI reduces merge interference at training time, with frozen random (near-orthogonal) A_t and sparse B_t. Pico is post-hoc and data-free on ordinary LoRAs.

methods.name: FrameFT
methods.full_name: FrameFT: fine-tuning with sparse coefficients in tight fusion frames
methods.paper_title: Fine-Tuning of Transformer models with Frames
methods.formula_latex: W=W_0+\Delta W,\ \ \Delta W=\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{d_{out}d_{in}}}\,P_{out}\,C\,P_{in}^{\top}=\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{d_{out}d_{in}}}\sum_{i=1}^{k}P_{out,i}\,C_i\,P_{in,i}^{\top};\ \ P_{out}=[P_{out,1},\dots,P_{out,k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times k\rho_{out}},\ P_{in}=[P_{in,1},\dots,P_{in,k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times k\rho_{in}}\ \ \text{(Parseval tight fusion frames from Spectral Tetris, } \textstyle\sum_iP_{\cdot,i}P_{\cdot,i}^{\top}=I\text{)};\ \ C=\mathrm{blockdiag}(C_1,\dots,C_k),\ C_i\in\mathbb{R}^{\rho_{out}\times\rho_{in}},\ \ \mathrm{supp}(C)=\Omega,\ |\Omega|=n_c \text{ random and shared by all layers};\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0,\ P_{out},\ P_{in},\ \Omega;\ \text{trained: the } n_c \text{ entries } C_{\Omega} \text{ of each adapted matrix}
methods.trainable_params: n_c\ \text{per adapted matrix } (n_c=1000 \text{ for RoBERTa, } 5000 \text{ for the 2B--13B LLMs, i.e. } 320\text{K in total on Llama-2-7B } W_q,W_v);\ \text{frames and support are regenerated from } (d,\rho) \text{ and a seed, so neither is stored}
methods.locus: W_q and W_v in every Transformer block (RoBERTa-base/large, Llama-2-7B/13B, Gemma-2-2B/9B, Llama-3.1-8B, ViT-B/L)
methods.structure: A fixed two-sided frame expansion with a sparse block-diagonal core. \(\Delta W=\sum_iP_{out,i}C_iP_{in,i}^{\top}\) couples the \(i\)-th output subspace only with the \(i\)-th input subspace, and only \(n_c\) core entries are free. Rank is not capped by a small \(r\): \(\mathrm{rank}\,\Delta W\le\mathrm{rank}\,C\le n_c\). The general definition allows redundant frames (\(k\rho>d\)). In every reported experiment, however, \(\rho=2\) and \(k\rho=d\) with Parseval normalisation. Then \(\sum_iP_iP_i^{\top}=I\) with ranks summing to \(d\) forces the subspaces to be mutually orthogonal, so \(P_{out}\) and \(P_{in}\) are square orthogonal matrices and the frame is not redundant. Running the released construct_real_tff at \(\rho=2\) confirms this: the matrix is orthogonal to about \(10^{-5}\) and dense (99.7 to 99.95% non-zeros for \(d=768\) to \(4096\)). The reason is that at \(\rho=2\) the Spectral Tetris unit-norm tight frame in \(\mathbb{C}^1\) is all ones, so the modulated frame is the realified \((d/2)\)-point DFT basis. In this regime FrameFT is FourierFT-like: sparse coefficients in a fixed DFT-type basis, with the support confined to small diagonal blocks. The block-sparse frames that the paper credits for compute savings appear only at larger \(\rho\). The released LLM scripts use \(4\times4\) coefficient blocks over the \(\rho=2\) subspaces. Lemma 3.1: if \(f(W)\) is \(L\)-smooth, the reparameterised loss \(f(C)\) is \(LB_{out}B_{in}\)-smooth, unlike LoRA's factored \((A,B)\) landscape. Gradient descent therefore gets the standard \(O(1/T)\) stationarity rate.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(\Delta W\) is a dense additive matrix computed from the frames and the sparse core. The released tuner's merge() adds it to \(W_0\), so inference cost is unchanged.
methods.identity_at_init: Yes. The released scripts set init_std=0, so \(C=0\) and \(\Delta W=0\); the tuner's reset routine also zeros the coefficients. The paper's Algorithm 1 only says 'Init'.
methods.key_idea: Replace LoRA's learned factor subspaces with fixed, algorithmically generated Parseval fusion frames, shared by all layers of the same width, and learn only a sparse block-diagonal coefficient matrix between them. Storage drops to \(n_c\) scalars per matrix, and the coefficient-space loss inherits the smoothness of the weight-space loss.
methods.results_note: Instruction-tuned on Alpaca with 320K trainable parameters, Llama-2-7B averages 63.62 on eight LM-eval-harness tasks, against 63.18 for LoRA (16.7M) and 63.22 for FourierFT (320K).

relations.note: Same recipe: a few trainable coefficients in a fixed basis shared across layers. In the reported setting (rho=2, k*rho=d), FrameFT's basis is itself a realified DFT, so the main difference is block-diagonal rather than scattered 2D-frequency support.
Sparse coefficients under a fixed wavelet synthesis instead of fusion frames.
Also a sparse core between fixed bases, but SVFT's bases are the singular vectors of W_0, stored per layer. FrameFT's bases depend only on (d, rho).
Core between frozen SVD bases of W_0. FrameFT replaces the weight-derived bases with data-independent frames.
On par or better on GLUE and Alpaca with 10-50x fewer trainable parameters.

methods.name: PrefixMemory-Tuning
methods.full_name: PrefixMemory-Tuning (PMT; titled Prefix-Tuning+ in arXiv v1 and v2)
methods.paper_title: PrefixMemory-Tuning: Modernizing Prefix-Tuning by Decoupling the Prefix from Attention
methods.formula_latex: \text{for each layer } l \text{ and attention head } h:\ \ o_i^{\top}=\frac{\sum_{j\le i}\mathrm{sim}(q_i,k_j)\,v_j^{\top}}{\sum_{j\le i}\mathrm{sim}(q_i,k_j)}+\phi(q_i)^{\top}M,\ \ q_i=W_Qx_i,\ k_j=W_Kx_j,\ v_j=W_Vx_j,\ \ \mathrm{sim}(q,k)=\exp\!\big(q^{\top}k/\sqrt{d_K}\big),\ \ \phi\in\{\mathrm{elu},\mathrm{gelu}\}\ \text{elementwise } (d_\phi=d_K),\ \ M\in\mathbb{R}^{d_\phi\times d_V};\ \ \text{derived from prefix-tuning with prefix } s_1,\dots,s_\ell \text{ by (i) taking the prefix out of the softmax with a fixed weight } \lambda,\ \text{(ii) linearising } \mathrm{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)\approx\phi(\cdot)^{\top}\phi(\cdot),\ \text{(iii) replacing } \textstyle\sum_{j\le\ell}\phi(W_Ks_j)(W_Vs_j)^{\top} \text{ by a free } M \text{, dropping the normaliser and absorbing } \lambda;\ \ \text{frozen: all base weights};\ \text{trained: } \{M_{l,h}\}
methods.trainable_params: L\cdot H\cdot d_\phi d_V\ \text{per model } (=L\,d\,d_K \text{ for multi-head attention with elementwise } \phi):\ 16.91\text{M } (0.25\%) \text{ on LLaMA2-7B-Chat, } 9.51\text{M } (0.31\%) \text{ on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct};\ \text{both reported counts exceed } LHd_Kd_V \text{ by exactly } L\cdot d\text{, consistent with one extra } d\text{-vector per layer that the text does not describe}
methods.locus: Every attention head of every layer: a query-conditioned branch added to each head's output before W_O (LLaMA2-7B-Chat, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-7B)
methods.structure: An additive, query-conditioned bias outside the softmax: \(o_i\mapsto o_i+M^{\top}\phi(q_i)\). Unlike a prefix, it is not renormalised against the input's attention mass. Prefix-tuning gives \(o^{pt}_i=(1-\alpha_i)o_i+\sum_{j\le\ell}\alpha_{ij}W_Vs_j\), where \(\alpha_i\) depends on the input and prefix lengths; this is the paper's tradeoff argument. In PMT the input path keeps weight 1 and the memory path is independent of length. A structural reading, derived here: through the frozen output projection, each layer gains the parallel branch \(\sum_hW_O^{(h)}M_h^{\top}\phi(W_Q^{(h)}x_i)\). That is a parallel bottleneck adapter whose down-projection is the frozen query projection \(W_Q^{(h)}\) (width \(d_K\) per head), whose nonlinearity is elu or gelu, and whose trained up-projection \(M_h^{\top}\) is read out through the frozen \(W_O\). It is the linear-kernel counterpart of He et al.'s view of prefix-tuning as a gated parallel adapter. Memory capacity scales with \(d_\phi\times d_V\) rather than with prefix length. Remark 1 notes that a trainable \(\phi_W(x)=\mathrm{ReLU}(Wx+b)\) would turn the branch into a one-hidden-layer MLP. The paper does not say whether \(q_i\) is taken before or after RoPE; after RoPE the branch would depend on position.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(\phi(q_i)^{\top}M\) is a non-linear (elu/gelu) function of the query, so the branch cannot be folded into \(W_Q,W_K,W_V\) or \(W_O\) and stays at inference. It costs about one extra \(d_K\times d_V\) product per head per token and does not grow the KV cache.
methods.identity_at_init: Not stated, and the linked code repository is empty. With \(M=0\) the branch vanishes and \(o^{PMT}_i=o_i\) exactly. Prefix-tuning has no such parameter value: any prefix with \(\ell\ge1\) takes softmax mass \(\alpha_i>0\) from the input.
methods.key_idea: Prefix-tuning underperforms on deep LLMs because the prefix shares each head's softmax normaliser with the input, so prefix influence and input specificity trade off with sequence length. PMT moves the prefix out of the softmax, linearises it with a kernel feature map \(\phi\), and replaces the prefix key-value sum with a free memory matrix \(M\), giving \(o_i=\mathrm{Attn}_i+\phi(q_i)^{\top}M\).
methods.results_note: With one training example per class, PMT reaches 71.2% on BigBench with LLaMA2-7B-Chat and 76.6% with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, above LoRA (r=64), prefix-tuning and full fine-tuning.

relations.note: Derived from the prefix-tuning attention output by decoupling the softmax, kernel-linearising, and freeing the prefix key-value sum. With the normaliser removed, prefix-tuning is not an exact member of the PMT family, so PMT relaxes it rather than strictly generalising it.

Starts from Petrov et al.'s decomposition o^pt = (1-alpha_i) o_i + sum_j alpha_ij W_V s_j. Argues that their explanation (prefixes cannot change the attention pattern) holds for shallow transformers but not for deep LLMs.

LLaMA-Adapter already gives adaption prompts their own softmax, separate from the token softmax, with a zero-init gate; this is PMT's step (i). PMT further linearises the prompt term and replaces it with a free matrix. The paper does not cite LLaMA-Adapter.
Derived here: through W_O, the PMT branch is a parallel adapter with a frozen down-projection W_Q^(h), an elementwise phi, and a trained up-projection M_h^T.
At a parameter budget comparable to LoRA r=32, PMT is ahead on few-shot classification, on CFT math and on AlpacaEval 2 win-rate deltas.

methods.name: FourTune
methods.full_name: FourTune: fully 4-bit (W4A4G4) LoRA post-training with a frozen low-rank numerical stabilizer
methods.paper_title: FourTune: Towards Fully 4-Bit Efficient Post-Training for Diffusion Models
methods.formula_latex: W_0\approx R+L_{\text{stab}},\ \ L_{\text{stab}}=L_1L_2\ \text{(low-rank outlier branch from the SVDQuant decomposition, kept in high precision)},\ \ R \text{ quantised offline to NVFP4 with } 16\times16 \text{ block scales};\ \ h=\mathrm{GEMM}_{4\text{bit}}\big(Q(R),Q(x)\big)+L_{\text{stab}}\,x+BA\,x;\ \ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=\mathrm{GEMM}_{4\text{bit}}\big(Q(R)^{\top},Q(g)\big)+L_{\text{stab}}^{\top}g+(BA)^{\top}g,\ \ g=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial h}\ \text{(4-bit gradients through the backbone; block scales let } Q(R)^{\top} \text{ be used without requantising)};\ \ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial B}=g\,(Ax)^{\top},\ \ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial A}=B^{\top}g\,x^{\top};\ \ \text{frozen: } R,\ L_{\text{stab}};\ \text{trained: } B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix } (r=64 \text{ in the experiments});\ \text{also frozen: the high-precision rank-}k \text{ stabilizer, } k(d_{in}+d_{out}) \text{ entries (} k \text{ not stated), and the 4-bit residual}
methods.locus: Linear layers (GEMMs) of the diffusion backbone: the FLUX.1-dev (12B) and Qwen-Image (20B) DiTs, plus SDXL. The MLP FC1 and FC2 kernels are fused.
methods.structure: A QLoRA-type composite with three parallel branches on each linear layer. The first is a frozen 4-bit residual GEMM (W4A4). The second is a frozen high-precision low-rank stabilizer \(L_{\text{stab}}\) that absorbs the quantisation-sensitive outlier directions of \(W_0\); this is SVDQuant's decomposition, reused here during training. The third is a trainable rank-\(r\) LoRA \(BA\). The trainable update is the ordinary additive \(BA\); what changes is the arithmetic. QLoRA dequantises and computes in W4A16G16, while FourTune runs the forward and input-gradient GEMMs in 4-bit (W4A4G4). Its \(16\times16\) block-wise scales let the transposed weight be used in the backward pass without requantisation. The LoRA down-projection, the stabilizer and activation quantisation share one fused kernel, and the 4-bit GEMM is fused with the up-projections. Without the stabilizer, naive W4A4G4 training shows gradient explosion (Fig. 8). The stabilizer and the LoRA have the same algebraic form (high-precision low-rank maps of \(x\)), so the trained LoRA can be concatenated into the stabilizer branch: \([L_1\ B][L_2;A]\).
methods.mergeable_reason: \(BA\) can be concatenated into the high-precision low-rank branch, \(L_{\text{stab}}+BA=[L_1\ B]\,[L_2;A]\) (rank \(k+r\)), which keeps the trained function exactly in a W4A4 inference engine. Folding it into the 4-bit residual \(R\) requires requantisation. Folding it into a BF16 \(W_0\) gives \(W_0+BA\), which differs from the training-time function by the quantisation error of \(R\).
methods.identity_at_init: Not stated. Under standard LoRA initialisation (\(BA=0\)) the model starts at the quantised base \(Q(R)Q(x)+L_{\text{stab}}x\approx W_0x\), not exactly at \(W_0x\).
methods.key_idea: FourTune aims to make PEFT faster than BF16 LoRA, not only smaller, by running the whole frozen backbone in native 4-bit for weights, activations and gradients. A frozen high-precision low-rank stabilizer \(L_{\text{stab}}\) carries the outlier directions. \(16\times16\) block scales and fused LoRA and MLP kernels keep the 4-bit backward pass efficient.
methods.results_note: In end-to-end FLUX.1-dev customization training, FourTune uses 14.51 GB against 29.35 GB for BF16 LoRA. A step takes 0.86 s on an RTX 5090, 2.27x faster than BF16 LoRA and 2.79x faster than NF4 QLoRA, at matched generation quality.

relations.note: Same design of a frozen 4-bit base plus LoRA. QLoRA dequantises for compute (W4A16G16); FourTune computes in W4A4G4.
Also NVFP4 base plus LoRA (QeRL targets RL for LLMs). QeRL dequantises weights for compute; FourTune quantises activations and gradients as well.
Both handle the quantised-base mismatch with a high-precision low-rank component. LoftQ puts it into the trainable LoRA initialisation; FourTune keeps it as a separate frozen stabilizer.
Training-time acceleration baseline for LoRA (contextual channel sparsity). It underperforms FourTune on pi-Flow distillation.
The trainable branch is a standard rank-64 LoRA.

methods.name: GradFix
methods.full_name: GradFix: gradient-sign masking for task-vector transport across pre-trained models
methods.paper_title: Gradient-Sign Masking for Task Vector Transport Across Pre-Trained Models
methods.formula_latex: \tau_A=\theta_A^{ft}-\theta_A\ \ (\text{per matrix } \Delta W_A=W_A^{ft}-W_A);\ \ \hat s_i=\mathrm{sign}\Big(-\sum_{(x_n,y_n)\in\mathcal{D}_s}\mathrm{sign}\big(\nabla_\theta\ell(f_{\theta_B}(x_n),y_n)\big)_i\Big)\ \ (\text{majority vote over } N=|\mathcal{D}_s| \text{ labelled target examples});\ \ m_i=\mathbb{1}\{\mathrm{sign}(\tau_{A,i})=\hat s_i\},\ \ \theta_B^{\text{trans}}=\theta_B+\alpha\,(m\odot\tau_A);\ \ \text{full-data form: } g=\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}(\theta_B),\ \ g^{\top}\big(\alpha\,m\odot\tau_A\big)=-\alpha\textstyle\sum_im_i|g_i||\tau_{A,i}|\le0;\ \ \text{frozen: } \theta_A,\ \theta_A^{ft},\ \theta_B;\ \text{nothing is trained; } \alpha \text{ is chosen on a validation set}
methods.trainable_params: 0\ \text{(training-free); each transport builds one binary mask } m\in\{0,1\}^{|\theta|} \text{ from } N \text{ per-sample target gradients, plus the scalar } \alpha
methods.locus: All parameters covered by the source task vector: the CLIP ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/14 image encoders (text encoder frozen), and the full T5-base model for language tasks
methods.structure: A coordinatewise Hadamard filter on a task vector, in parameter coordinates. The transported delta keeps \(\tau_A\) on the sign-agreement set \(\{i:\mathrm{sign}\,\tau_{A,i}=\mathrm{sign}(-g_i)\}\) unchanged and zeros it elsewhere. This makes it a base-change map: a displacement measured at base point \(\theta_A\) is projected onto the target's local descent orthant at \(\theta_B\), with no permutation alignment and no parameter updates. The first-order descent property holds by construction. With few samples it holds with high probability, because the majority-vote sign concentrates (Hoeffding: \(\Pr[\hat s_i=\mathrm{sign}(-g_i)]\ge1-e^{-2N(p_i-1/2)^2}\)). The filter acts on coordinates, not on functions, so it depends on the basis. One consequence, derived here: for a factored adapter, \(m\odot(BA)\) is in general full-rank, so a LoRA task vector would be transported as a masked dense matrix, not as low-rank factors. The paper's experiments use full fine-tuning task vectors. For multi-task merging, merge-then-mask with a consensus target-sign mask works best; for several sources fine-tuned on one task, mask-then-merge works best. Magnitude-weighted masks underperform, which the paper reads as directions transferring across pre-trainings while magnitudes do not.
methods.mergeable_reason: The result is a single additive weight delta \(\alpha\,m\odot\tau_A\) on \(\theta_B\). It composes with Task Arithmetic and TIES (mask-then-merge or merge-then-mask) and adds no inference overhead.
methods.identity_at_init: Nothing is trained. \(\alpha=0\), or an empty mask, returns the target base \(\theta_B\) exactly.
methods.key_idea: A task vector trained on an old base \(\theta_A\) transfers to a new release \(\theta_B\) once its coordinates whose sign disagrees with the target's anti-gradient are removed. A few target gradients, combined by a majority vote of signs and with no update steps, rebase \(\tau_A\) onto \(\theta_B\) with a first-order descent guarantee \(g^{\top}\delta\le0\).
methods.results_note: With one labelled example per class, transporting a DataComp-XL CLIP ViT-B/16 EuroSAT task vector to a LAION-2B ViT-B/16 gives 61.94%. Naive task-vector addition gives 49.58%, zero-shot 49.41%, and few-shot fine-tuning on the same samples 56.61%.

relations.note: Extends task-vector addition to a different base point. Naive theta_B + tau_A stays near zero-shot when the bases differ.
Used with TA and TIES in multi-task merging (merge-then-mask) and multi-source merging (mask-then-merge). TIES elects signs by task-vector mass; GradFix elects them by target anti-gradient votes.
Both move fine-tuning knowledge to a new base model. Trans-LoRA re-trains the adapter by distillation on synthetic data; GradFix is training-free masking from a few labelled samples.
Both are training-free cross-model transfer. LoRA-X projects onto the target's SVD subspaces; GradFix applies a coordinatewise gradient-sign mask.

notes: All six requested methods exist, all are PEFT or PEFT-composition methods, and none duplicates a catalogued id. I checked existing_index.json and every JSON file under research/. PrefixMemory-Tuning (called Prefix-Tuning+ in arXiv v1 and v2) had earlier been listed as EXCLUDED in frontier.json for low uptake. It is added now as an ICLR 2026 paper with 5 Semantic Scholar citations. Venues come from the official virtual-site JSON downloaded on 2026-10-02: AR1-ZO is a NeurIPS 2026 poster (OpenReview 7eOsaBX3qO). Pico is a NeurIPS 2026 poster (PtEkosDXWk). FrameFT is an ICML 2026 poster (KCfbSVIheg). FourTune is an ICML 2026 poster (RpwnrBkht2). PrefixMemory-Tuning is an ICLR 2026 poster (LvUMpZE44r). GradFix is an ICLR 2026 poster (CQnpxZNMvT). Year follows the first public version: PrefixMemory-Tuning is 2025 (arXiv v1 on 2025-06-16), GradFix is 2025 (v1 on 2025-10-07), and the other four are 2026. Semantic Scholar citation counts on 2026-10-02: AR1-ZO 0, Pico 0, FrameFT 0, PrefixMemory-Tuning 5, FourTune 1, GradFix 3. None of the six is in HF PEFT v0.21.2 (2026-10-01). FrameFT ships its own patched peft with a 'frame' tuner. Formulas were read from the arXiv HTML method sections, and for FrameFT also from the released tuner code. Corrections to the sweep reasons. (1) AR1-ZO: 'directional collapse' is the Theta(r^-2) decay of the finite-difference SNR caused by inheriting the alpha/r coefficient under single-atom queries. It is a measurement-scale effect, not a statement about the cone geometry of BA. (2) Pico: the claim that it is the 'first merging rule built on the A/B asymmetry' is not supported. LoRI (catalogued) already exploits A/B roles to limit merge interference, and KnOTS and Core Space already work with the factor spaces separately. What is new in Pico is calibrating only B by spectral energy share before merging. For Task Arithmetic, Pico reduces exactly to a post-merge left multiplication by S. (3) FrameFT: every reported experiment uses rho=2 and k*rho=d with Parseval frames. That frame is a non-redundant orthogonal basis, not a redundant non-orthogonal dictionary. I checked numerically that the released construct_real_tff at rho=2 returns a dense matrix, orthogonal to about 1e-5, which is the realified (d/2)-point DFT basis. So in practice FrameFT is close to FourierFT with block-diagonal support. Redundancy appears only in the general definition (k*rho>d). (4) PrefixMemory-Tuning: the prompts-family axis change can be stated concretely. PMT has an identity point (M=0) that prefix-tuning lacks. Structurally it is a parallel adapter whose down-projection is the frozen W_Q (my derivation). LLaMA-Adapter's separately normalised, gated prompt softmax already anticipated PMT's step (i), and the paper does not cite it. The code link printed in the paper (github.com/haonan3/PrefixMemory-Tuning) is an empty repository, created 2026-04-18. Initialisation, pre- or post-RoPE queries, and the extra L*d parameters implied by Table 8 therefore cannot be checked. That is why code_url is empty and confidence is medium. (5) FourTune: the abstract's 2.25x memory figure comes from Fig. 1. The body reports 2.02x end-to-end (14.51 vs 29.35 GB) and 2.93x for DiT weights alone. The 2.27x figure is the step-time speedup on an RTX 5090. The paper does not state the stabilizer rank or the LoRA initialisation. (6) GradFix: its task vectors are full fine-tuning deltas (Ilharco et al. protocol), not LoRA. It is included as a training-free base-change (transport) composition method. No theory-only papers were in this batch, so papers is empty. Semantic Scholar first returned HTTP 429; the batch endpoint worked on retry. Metadata comes from arxiv.org/abs pages, so the arXiv export API was not needed.
